{"verdict": "true-positive", "reason": "The Express handler at server.ts:3 takes req.body.email and saves it with User.create for the '/marketing' purpose without checking consent on the server. The only consent check is client-side, in frontend/src/app/campaign.component.ts:2 (`if (this.consent)`), and a direct POST to /marketing skips it completely. The server stores the contact data without verifying that the user agreed to marketing, so it has no proof of consent for this purpose. The supplied evidence doesn't point to any legitimate-use basis either. This matches the positive CON-01 example, and differs from the negative example only in the missing server-side `if (!req.body.consent) return 403` guard.", "citations": ["DPDP-Act-4(1)", "DPDP-Act-6(1)"]}

{"verdict": "true-positive", "reason": "The evidence at frontend/src/index.html:1 shows a consent checkbox (name=\"consent\") with the `checked` attribute, so consent is ticked before the user does anything. This is the same as the supplied positive example for CON-03. Section 6(1) requires consent to be unambiguous and given by a clear affirmative action. A pre-ticked box means the user's agreement is assumed, not given by an action they take, which fails that standard. The checkbox collects consent for Profile data, and the 'Internal-Restricted' exposure does not change the consent requirement. One caveat: the rule name says 'angular-default-true', but the evidence is a plain HTML `checked` attribute rather than an Angular binding. The defect is the same either way, so the finding stands.", "citations": ["DPDP-Act-6(1)", "DPDP-Act-6"]}

{"verdict": "true-positive", "reason": "On line 3 of server.ts, POST /marketing sends req.body.email to an outside Data Processor (https://processor.example/send). It does not check whether consent was given. On line 4, DELETE /consent only sets the local Consent record to granted: false. It never tells the processor to stop processing or to erase the email it already received, and no other code in the Evidence does this either. Section 6(6) requires the Fiduciary to make its Data Processors stop processing after consent is withdrawn. Section 8(7)(b) requires it to make them erase the data it shared. Under Section 8(1), the Fiduciary is also responsible for processing done on its behalf. The code matches the positive CON-05 example exactly. The negative example differs because its withdrawal handler calls the processor's erase endpoint.", "citations": ["DPDP-Act-6(6)", "DPDP-Act-8(7)", "DPDP-Act-8(7)(b)", "DPDP-Act-8"]}

{"verdict": "true-positive", "reason": "The route is declared with @router.get('/gravatar'), and its handler is `get_gravatar(email: str, user=Depends(get_verified_user))`. In FastAPI, a plain scalar parameter like `email: str` that isn't part of the path becomes a query parameter. So the user's email address, which is contact personal data, travels in the GET request's URL query string. URLs like this get written to web server and proxy access logs, browser history and referrer headers. The handler then passes the email to get_gravatar_url and returns the result. This matches the positive example (GET with req.query.email), not the negative one (POST with the email in the body). Requiring a verified user limits who can call the endpoint, but the email still ends up in the URL. This is a case of sensitive data in a GET query string (CWE-598), and it falls short of the reasonable security safeguards, such as masking or obfuscation, that Rule 6(1)(a) expects. A fix would be to accept the email in a POST body, or have the client send a hash.", "citations": ["CWE-598", "DPDP-Rule-6(1)(a)", "DPDP-Rule-6(1)"]}
